name: Pulmonary atresia
aliases: pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum
pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect

clinicalPearls: Complete obstruction of the right ventricular outflow to the pulmonary arteries, so there is no antegrade pulmonary blood flow
It occurs with an intact ventricular septum or with a ventricular septal defect, which differ in physiology and management
Pulmonary blood flow is duct-dependent, so neonates become profoundly cyanotic as the duct closes
In the intact-septum form the right ventricle is often hypoplastic and may have coronary sinusoids or right-ventricle-dependent coronary circulation
The form with a ventricular septal defect resembles severe tetralogy of Fallot and may have major aortopulmonary collaterals
Prostaglandin to maintain the duct is the immediate priority, followed by staged surgical or catheter intervention
reference.pathophysiology: In pulmonary atresia there is no patent pathway from the right ventricle to the pulmonary arteries, so pulmonary perfusion depends on the arterial duct or on aortopulmonary collateral arteries. With an intact ventricular septum, blood cannot leave the right ventricle, which becomes hypertensive and often hypoplastic, sometimes maintaining fistulous connections (sinusoids) to the coronary arteries; closure of the duct causes life-threatening hypoxaemia. With a ventricular septal defect, the right ventricle decompresses through the defect and pulmonary supply comes from the duct or collaterals, giving a spectrum that overlaps with severe tetralogy of Fallot.
additionalDifferentials: Ebstein anomaly with functional pulmonary atresia
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography defining outflow obstruction and ventricular size
Assessment for coronary sinusoids and right-ventricle-dependent coronary circulation
Imaging of pulmonary arteries and any aortopulmonary collaterals
redFlags: Profound cyanosis as the duct closes
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the subtype and pulmonary artery and right ventricular anatomy; many children require staged intervention, achieving biventricular or single-ventricle circulations with variable long-term results.
pitfalls: Decompressing a right ventricle that supplies the coronary circulation, causing ischaemia
Confusing the two subtypes, which need different strategies
